title: What If You Jumped on a Cloud? ☁️
description:
Gus stares at a fat little cloud and decides it is the softest bed in the world. So he puts on a parachute, borrows a balloon and jumps on it.

The numbers:
• A small fair-weather cloud holds about 0.5 gram of water in every cubic metre. One cubic kilometre of it: 500 metric tons, 1.1 million pounds, about a hundred 5-ton elephants.
• The same number, small: a piece the size of a big fridge (1 cubic metre) holds half a gram, ten drops. The air in that piece weighs about 2,000 times more than its water.
• A cloud droplet is about 20 micrometres across and sinks about half an inch (1.2 cm) a second, so the gentlest rising air holds it up. Fog is the same thing at ground level.
• An 80 kg jumper who steps off at the top falls through a kilometre of cloud in about 22 seconds, speeding up toward 120 mph. The water in his path: about 250 grams, one cup.
• It takes about a million cloud droplets to make one raindrop.
(Assumptions: a cube-shaped cloud 1 km on a side, the example of the US Geological Survey; a belly-down fall; one cup is what lies in his path, and much of it flows around him. Thunderclouds are far bigger and wetter. Real skydivers have to stay clear of clouds, because nobody can see through one.)

Sources:
• USGS Water Science School, "How much does a cloud weigh?" (0.5 g per cubic metre, 1.1 million pounds)
• Library of Congress, Everyday Mysteries, "How much does a cloud weigh?"
• Atmospheric Processes and Phenomena (University of Hawaii), chapter 7: cloud droplets and raindrops
• FAI Skydiving Commission and USPA Skydiver's Information Manual: belly-to-earth fall speed, about 120 mph
• Stokes' law for the sinking speed of a droplet

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
